name: Self-Driving Laboratories
title: Self-Driving Laboratories
answer: Self-driving laboratories combine robotic hardware, automated instruments, and machine learning to plan and run experiments with limited human intervention. They are used in materials discovery, chemical synthesis, formulation, and biological assay work. The goal is to close the loop between proposing an experiment, executing it, measuring the result, and using that result to choose the next experiment. This shifts the researcher's role from manual bench work to setting objectives and constraints.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Self-driving laboratories combine robotic hardware, automated instruments, and machine learning to plan and run experiments with limited human intervention. They are used in materials discovery, chemical synthesis, formulation, and biological assay work. The goal is to close the loop between proposing an experiment, executing it, measuring the result, and using that result to choose the next experiment. This shifts the researcher's role from manual bench work to setting objectives and constraints.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A self-driving lab typically runs on a robotic liquid handler or solid dispensing system, analytical instruments such as spectrometers or chromatographs, and a software layer that coordinates them. The control software often sits on a local server or cloud instance and communicates with instruments through standard interfaces like SiLA or vendor APIs. Data from each run is stored in a structured database or electronic lab notebook so the learning algorithm can access it. Some labs use modular hardware that can be reconfigured for different workflows.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by an iterative loop of design, execution, and analysis. A machine learning model, often Bayesian optimization or a Gaussian process, proposes the next set of experimental conditions based on prior results. The robotic system then prepares samples, runs the measurement, and returns the outcome to the model. This active learning approach aims to find high performing materials or conditions in fewer experiments than a grid or random search. Human scientists review the proposed experiments and can override unsafe or impractical suggestions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on data ownership, reproducibility, and safety. Because the system generates large volumes of experimental data automatically, clear records of who can access and reuse that data are needed. Provenance requires logging every step, including instrument calibration, reagent batch, and software version, so results can be audited. Risk includes chemical or biological hazards from unattended operation, and the possibility that a model optimizes for a narrow metric while missing a broader failure mode. No legal or safety standard is implied here; practice varies by institution.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going is toward more general and more autonomous systems that can handle multi step synthesis, characterization, and even hypothesis generation. Researchers are working on transferring knowledge between different materials or reaction spaces so a lab does not start from zero for each new problem. There is also interest in connecting several self-driving labs into shared facilities with common data formats. The long term aim is to make experimental science faster and more reproducible, while keeping human judgment in the loop for goals and ethics.
